report:
## Conclusion: Yes — the evidence supports it

For heavy current or former smokers who meet screening eligibility criteria, regular participation in low-dose CT (LDCT) lung cancer screening reduces lung cancer mortality, based on multiple large randomized controlled trials.

**Key evidence:**

1. **NLST (National Lung Screening Trial, US, ~53,000 participants):** This landmark RCT found that annual LDCT screening reduced lung cancer mortality by 20% compared with chest X-ray in older, heavy smokers (30+ pack-years, current or quit within 15 years) — the first trial of adequate size/power to demonstrate this benefit ([cancer.gov](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/research/nlst); [ilcn.org](https://www.ilcn.org/what-have-we-learned-from-the-national-lung-screening-trial/)).

2. **NELSON trial (Netherlands/Belgium, ~15,800 heavy smokers):** Using volume-based LDCT screening, this trial found a 24% reduction in lung cancer mortality in men and a 33% reduction in the smaller subgroup of women after 10 years of follow-up, confirming and extending the NLST findings in a European population ([theclinicaltimes.com](https://theclinicaltimes.com/landmarks/2020-nelson-lung-cancer-screening-trial); techtimes.com summary).

3. **Broader synthesis:** A health-technology assessment and review literature conclude that "systematic lung cancer screening with low-dose CT lowers mortality from lung cancer in (current or former) heavy smokers," while noting this benefit must be weighed against real harms — false positives, overdiagnosis, and cumulative radiation exposure ([di.aerzteblatt.de](https://di.aerzteblatt.de/int/archive/article/231736)).

**Caveats:** Benefit is specific to high-risk heavy smokers meeting trial-defined criteria (age, pack-years, quit-time), and screening must be sustained across multiple annual rounds to achieve the mortality benefit; not all smaller RCTs individually reached statistical significance, though combined evidence and the two largest, adequately powered trials (NLST, NELSON) are consistent and are the basis for current screening guidelines.
